definition: In this historical source, the motor tract refers to the part of the brain associated with large ganglionic motor cells and movement-related function. It is discussed as a site where these cells may undergo disease changes in epilepsy.

reasons: The packet only says there are “large ganglionic cells of the motor tract”; it does not support defining the motor tract itself as a specific part of the brain or as having movement-related function.

The epilepsy sentence overstates the source: it reports diseased changes in cells of the motor tract in some cases of epileptic insanity, not that the motor tract as such is a site where these cells may undergo disease changes in epilepsy.

The phrase “movement-related function” is not explicitly supported by the packet text; the excerpt mentions “large ganglionic cells of the motor tract” but does not directly describe movement-related function in these terms.

The definition’s wording that “the motor tract refers to the part of the brain associated with large ganglionic motor cells” is only partially supported: the packet says there is a “large ganglionic … of the motor tract” but it does not clearly define the motor tract as a specific “part of the brain” beyond that reference.

While the packet supports that these cells are discussed as having a “diseased condition” in relation to epilepsy (“in the brains of the epileptic insane,” and “diseased condition … of the … large ganglionic cells of the motor tract”), the definition includes additional interpretive phrasing (“movement-related function,” “part of the brain associated with”) that goes beyond what is stated.
